title: Work Extraction Across a Thermodynamic Hierarchy in Quantum Many-Body Systems
abstract: Thermodynamics is operational in the sense that the very concept of thermal equilibrium depends crucially on the choice of observables, while the amount of extractable work is defined relative to the allowed operations. Here we show that isolated quantum many-body states admit a thermodynamic hierarchical structure of observables and allowed operations, where the same state can be thermal at one level of the hierarchy and athermal at another. Enlarging the set of allowed operations therefore renders such hidden athermality a potential resource for work extraction; the resulting work gain is bounded in terms of the difference between the entropy densities of the two levels. This entropy difference takes the form of the mutual-information density. We establish the bounds for three extensions of operational access: increased spatial resolution, increased duration of control, and nonlocal connectivity, which provide access to position-state Holevo information, correlations between neighboring regions and spatially nonlocal correlations, respectively. Thus the difference between entropies at different levels of the thermodynamic hierarchy governs the bound on the work gain associated with moving to a less restricted level.
summary: This paper develops a thermodynamic hierarchy for quantum many-body systems, showing that the amount of extractable work depends on the allowed set of operations. The key finding is that the excess work is bounded by the difference in entropy densities between the restricted and expanded operational levels. This provides a powerful, information-theoretic tool to quantify hidden work resources in quantum matter.
main_problem: The paper investigates the thermodynamic hierarchical structure of observables and allowed operations in isolated quantum many-body systems.
main_result: The extractable work when enlarging the set of allowed operations is bounded by the difference between the entropy densities of the restricted and enlarged operational levels.
method: The authors establish quantitative bounds by relating work extraction to the difference in entropy functionals (e.g., mutual information density, Holevo information) across different operational regimes.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on isolated quantum many-body states ($ho$) on a lattice, considering various operational constraints such as spatial resolution, control duration, and non-local connectivity.
key_observables: Extractable Work Density, Entropy Densities ($s_R, s_E$), Mutual-Information Density, Holevo Information, Total Correlation.
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($ eta$), system size ($L$), spatial resolution ($l$), and the difference between entropy levels.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes cyclic operations with no heat exchange, and later sections rely on the existence of thermodynamic limits and decay properties of interaction profiles.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates work extraction across thermodynamic levels, bounded by the entropy difference. Figure 2 illustrates work gain across different spatial scales, relating it to entropy differences.
paper_structure: The paper develops the concept of a thermodynamic hierarchy, first establishing general bounds on work extraction based on entropy differences, and then applying this framework to specific physical extensions like increased spatial resolution or nonlocal connectivity.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, information-theoretic framework for quantifying non-equilibrium work extraction in quantum systems, directly linking thermodynamic potential differences to quantum information measures.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of extractable work across thermodynamic levels. Consider a quantum state ρ that is in thermal equilibrium at a specific thermodynamic level (the “restricted” level), i.e., with respect to a given observational resolution and a compatible class of operations. At this level, the entropy sR(ρ) equals the thermodynamic entropy, and Planck’s principle prohibits work extraction from this state via an adiabatic cycle. With a higher observational resolution and a broader class of operations (the “enlarged” level), the same state ρ may become out of equilibrium. FIG. 2. Three methods to extract work by enlarging the control class. (a) A spatially varying configuration can become thermal after positional averaging, yet local access to microscopic position enables one to utilize the position-state Holevo information to extract additional work. (b) Individual small cells appear thermal, although their union need not, owing to inter-cell correlations; a longer short-range operation can resolve the larger cell to extract additional work. FIG. 3. Equally-separated entangled-pair (ESEP) state and its entropy landscape across varying scales. (a) A segment of |ESEPl⟩: every site belongs to a singlet Bell pair whose endpoints are separated by l sites. Any contiguous interval of length r ≤l contains no complete pair and is therefore maximally mixed, appearing thermal at β = 0. (b) The entropy of a region of length r follows the thermal value r ln 2 up to the pairing scale l and equals (l + O(1)) ln 2 for l ≤r ≤L/2. The nonlocal pair correlations give rise to the entropy difference shown in the shaded region.
